issues.legal_issue: An appeal is maintainable when it is brought by an interested entity that was not a party to an earlier special leave petition concerning the same order.
material_facts: The housing board had acquired the property and had its own interest in challenging orders affecting it.
A separate company had earlier filed a special leave petition concerning the High Court order, which was withdrawn with liberty to seek review in the High Court.
The housing board had not been a party to that earlier special leave petition.
issues.conclusion: The housing board’s appeals were maintainable; the earlier withdrawal by the separate company did not bar them.
issues.legal_principle: The restrictions discussed in Kumaran Silk Trade (P.) Ltd. v. Devendra (2007) 12 SCC 549, and the rule in Order 47 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning appeals from rejection of review, did not bar an appeal by an entity that was not a party to the earlier proceedings and had not itself challenged the order. The Court distinguished Shanker Motiram Nale v. Shiolalsing Gannusing Rajput (1994) 2 SCC 753, Vinod Kapoor v. State of Goa (2012) 12 SCC 378, and M.N. Haider v. Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (2004) 13 SCC 677.

predicates.appeal_from_order: An entity brought an appeal challenging an order made in earlier proceedings.
predicates.appellant_not_party_to_earlier_special_l: The appealing entity was not a party to an earlier special leave petition concerning the order.
predicates.appellant_own_interest_affected: The order affected an interest held by the appealing entity.

issues.definition: When an entity appeals an order affecting its own interest despite not having been a party to an earlier special leave petition about that order, its appeal is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An interim injunction cannot bind or be enforced through police assistance against a purchaser whose vendors were not parties to the suit in which the injunction was made.
material_facts: The suit had abated against the prior owner, and the prior owner’s heirs were not joined as parties.
The property was added to the suit schedule after the suit began, without joining the heirs.
The housing board purchased the property from those heirs and was not a party to the suit.
An interim injunction and directions for police assistance were made in relation to the property.
issues.conclusion: The interim injunction did not bind the housing board, and police assistance could not be used to enforce it against the board, its agents, or persons claiming through it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, an injunction may be granted only against parties to the suit; a purported consent order binds only those parties. The Court also accepted that the property had not been transferred by a party to the suit, and therefore the respondents’ reliance on the lis pendens principle in Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, did not make the injunction enforceable against the purchaser.

rule.if: civil_suit_with_interim_injunction and property_added_to_suit_after_commencement and purchaser_not_party_to_suit and vendors_not_parties_to_suit

predicates.civil_suit_with_interim_injunction: A civil suit included an interim injunction concerning property.
predicates.property_added_to_suit_after_commencemen: The property was added to the suit after the suit had commenced.
predicates.purchaser_not_party_to_suit: The entity that purchased the property was not a party to the suit.
predicates.vendors_not_parties_to_suit: The persons who transferred the property to the purchaser were not parties to the suit.

issues.definition: If property is added to a civil suit after commencement and both its purchaser and vendors are outside the suit, an interim injunction in that suit cannot bind or be enforced against the purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction to include land in a partition suit when the relevant rights are governed by a statutory land-settlement scheme and fall within matters reserved from civil-court adjudication.
material_facts: The prior owner had retained intermediary rights in the land under the statutory estate-settlement scheme.

The heirs’ rights were reflected in the record of rights following proceedings concerning retention of the land, and that result was affirmed by the Supreme Court in West Bengal Government Employees (Food and Supplies) Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. Sulekha Pal (Dey), (2003) 9 SCC 253.
The property was added to a civil partition suit, although the heirs were not parties to it.
issues.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to deal with the property, and adding it to the partition suit was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Section 57B(2)(a), (b) and (c) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 bars civil courts from entertaining suits or applications concerning matters including alteration of finally published land records, disputes about entitlement to retain land under the Act, and matters assigned for inquiry or determination to the State Government or its authorities. Section 6 provides for the relevant retention rights. The Court relied on Sulekha Pal for the determination that the heirs’ rights in the land had been retained and recorded.

predicates.civil_partition_suit: A civil court is asked to include land in a partition suit.
predicates.land_rights_settled_under_statutory_sche: The land rights were settled under a statutory scheme governing retention of land.
predicates.heirs_rights_entered_in_land_record: The heirs’ rights in the land were entered in the relevant land record.
predicates.dispute_concerns_matter_reserved_to_admi: The dispute concerns a matter that the statutory scheme assigns to an administrative authority rather than a civil court.

issues.definition: When a civil partition suit concerns land whose statutory rights have been settled and recorded in a matter reserved to an administrative authority, the civil court lacks jurisdiction over that land.
